notes.front: What does TOGAF stand for, and who maintains it?
notes.back: The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF). It is developed and maintained by The Open Group, an industry consortium. TOGAF is a framework and method for Enterprise Architecture (EA).

notes.front: When was the TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition released, and what was its defining change versus the 9.2 edition?
notes.back: Released April 2022. Defining change: the standard was restructured into a modular form — a stable Fundamental Content plus a flexible body of Series Guides (the TOGAF Library) — instead of one monolithic document. The core method itself was largely unchanged.

notes.front: What are the four architecture domains in TOGAF?
notes.back:
• Business Architecture
  • Data Architecture
  • Application Architecture
  • Technology Architecture
Data + Application together form the Information Systems Architectures. Mnemonic: BDAT.

notes.front: Name the six documents of the TOGAF 10 Fundamental Content.
notes.back:
1. Introduction and Core Concepts
  2. Architecture Development Method (ADM)
  3. ADM Techniques
  4. Applying the ADM
  5. Architecture Content
  6. Enterprise Architecture Capability and Governance

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Library?
notes.back: A reference library of guidance, templates, and techniques — the TOGAF Series Guides — that supports applying the standard. In the 10th edition it holds the flexible content, kept separate from the stable Fundamental Content.

notes.front: What are the main functional components of the TOGAF framework?
notes.back:
• Architecture Development Method (ADM)
  • ADM Guidelines & Techniques
  • Architecture Content Framework
  • Enterprise Continuum & Tools
  • Architecture Capability Framework

notes.front: In TOGAF, what two senses of the word "architecture" are recognised?
notes.back: (1) A formal description/detailed plan of a system to guide its implementation; and (2) the structure of components, their interrelationships, and the principles/guidelines governing their design and evolution over time.

notes.front: What is the purpose of Enterprise Architecture (EA) according to TOGAF?
notes.back: To optimise across the enterprise the often fragmented legacy of processes (manual and automated) into an integrated environment that is responsive to change and supportive of the business strategy. It aligns IT and business and reduces risk and cost.

notes.front: List the phases of the Architecture Development Method (ADM) in order.
notes.back: Preliminary → A Architecture Vision → B Business Architecture → C Information Systems Architectures → D Technology Architecture → E Opportunities & Solutions → F Migration Planning → G Implementation Governance → H Architecture Change Management. Requirements Management sits at the centre, operating throughout.

notes.front: What sits at the centre of the ADM cycle, and why?
notes.back: Requirements Management. It is a continuous process — not a phase with a fixed position — because every phase both feeds requirements into and draws requirements from the requirements repository.

notes.front: What are the four iteration cycles defined for the ADM?
notes.back:
• Architecture Capability iteration (Preliminary + Phase A work)
  • Architecture Development iteration (Phases B–D)
  • Transition Planning iteration (Phases E–F)
  • Architecture Governance iteration (Phases G–H)

notes.front: In the ADM, what is the difference between the Baseline and Target Architectures?
notes.back: The Baseline ("as-is") describes the existing architecture; the Target ("to-be") describes the desired future architecture. The gap between them drives the work packages in the Architecture Roadmap.

notes.front: Objective of the Preliminary Phase of the ADM?
notes.back: To prepare and initiate the organisation to do successful Enterprise Architecture — establishing the Architecture Capability: tailoring the framework, defining Architecture Principles, selecting tools, and setting up governance. Answers "where, what, why, who, and how we do architecture."

notes.front: Key outputs of the Preliminary Phase?
notes.back:
• Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture
  • Tailored Architecture Framework (incl. Architecture Principles)
  • Initial Architecture Repository
  • Restated business principles, goals, and drivers
  • Architecture Governance framework
  • (Possibly) a Request for Architecture Work

notes.front: Objective of Phase A: Architecture Vision?
notes.back: To develop a high-level aspirational vision of the capabilities and business value to be delivered; obtain approval for a Statement of Architecture Work; and define scope, stakeholders, and constraints. It is the project-initiation phase of an architecture cycle.

notes.front: Key deliverables of Phase A?
notes.back:
• Statement of Architecture Work (approved)
  • Architecture Vision
  • Refined Architecture Principles
  • Capability Assessment
  • Communications Plan
  • Tailored Architecture Framework
Trigger/input: Request for Architecture Work.

notes.front: Which technique is commonly used in Phase A to discover and document the business vision and requirements?
notes.back: Business Scenarios — used to identify and understand business needs and the people, systems, and processes involved, ensuring the architecture is driven by real requirements.

notes.front: Objective of Phase B: Business Architecture?
notes.back: To develop the Target Business Architecture describing how the enterprise must operate to achieve its business goals and the Architecture Vision, and to identify gaps between the Baseline and Target Business Architectures.

notes.front: Which four foundational TOGAF Series Guides support Business Architecture work?
notes.back:
• Business Capabilities
  • Value Streams
  • Organization Mapping
  • Information Mapping (with Business Models guidance)

notes.front: What does Phase C of the ADM cover?
notes.back: The Information Systems Architectures: the Data Architecture and the Application Architecture. They may be developed in either order or in parallel.

notes.front: Objective of the Data Architecture (part of Phase C)?
notes.back: To define the types and sources of data needed to support the business — in a way that is understandable to stakeholders, complete, consistent, and stable. It is concerned with data entities, not database design.

notes.front: Objective of the Application Architecture (part of Phase C)?
notes.back: To define the major kinds of application systems needed to process the data and support the business — describing them as logical groups of capability, independent of specific technology/products.

notes.front: Objective of Phase D: Technology Architecture?
notes.back: To define the Target Technology Architecture — the logical and physical technology components (hardware, software, infrastructure, communications) that enable the application and data components and realise the Architecture Vision.

notes.front: Objective of Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions?
notes.back: To generate the initial complete Architecture Roadmap; identify delivery vehicles (projects, programs, portfolios); and decide whether an incremental approach is needed, defining Transition Architectures if so. It is the first phase directly concerned with implementation.

notes.front: What is a Transition Architecture?
notes.back: A formal description of the enterprise architecture at a specific point in time between the Baseline and Target — an intermediate, deliverable state used to manage incremental delivery of business value.

notes.front: Objective of Phase F: Migration Planning?
notes.back: To finalise the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan; coordinate them with the enterprise's change-management and portfolio processes; and prioritise projects via cost/benefit and risk assessment.

notes.front: Objective of Phase G: Implementation Governance?
notes.back: To provide architectural oversight of implementation — ensuring that solution delivery conforms to the Target Architecture, governed through Architecture Contracts.

notes.front: Which document binds development partners and sponsors to the architecture during implementation (Phase G)?
notes.back: The Architecture Contract — a joint agreement governing deliverables, quality, and fitness-for-purpose, enabling governance to ensure compliance with the architecture.

notes.front: Objective of Phase H: Architecture Change Management?
notes.back: To ensure the architecture lifecycle is maintained; to establish procedures for managing change to the new architecture; and to determine whether a change warrants a new ADM cycle.

notes.front: In Phase H, what distinguishes an incremental/simplification change from one requiring a new architecture definition?
notes.back: A change with broad, strategic impact across many stakeholders may require a full new ADM cycle, whereas changes that fit within the existing architecture framework are handled as incremental change requests or simplification changes.

notes.front: Objective of Requirements Management in the ADM?
notes.back: To manage architecture requirements throughout the ADM — identifying, storing, and feeding them into and out of every phase. Note: it does not itself dispose of, address, or prioritise requirements; that happens within the relevant phases.

notes.front: What three categories of architectural work products does the Architecture Content Framework define?
notes.back:
• Deliverables — contractually specified, formally reviewed and signed off
  • Artifacts — granular work products describing an architecture (catalogs, matrices, diagrams)
  • Building Blocks — reusable components of capability

notes.front: Difference between an Architecture Building Block (ABB) and a Solution Building Block (SBB)?
notes.back: An ABB defines required capability and shapes the specification of SBBs (the what — technology/vendor-neutral). An SBB is a concrete component or product implementation that meets the business need (the how).

notes.front: What are the three types of artifacts in the Content Framework, with an example of each?
notes.back:
• Catalogs — lists of building blocks (e.g., Technology Standards Catalog)
  • Matrices — relationships between building blocks (e.g., Business Interaction Matrix)
  • Diagrams — visual renderings (e.g., Business Footprint Diagram)

notes.front: Relationship between Stakeholders, Concerns, Views, and Viewpoints (per TOGAF / ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010)?
notes.back: Stakeholders hold Concerns. A Viewpoint defines the conventions for constructing and using a view (the template/perspective). A View is what a stakeholder actually sees, addressing related concerns. Memory aid: a view is what you see; a viewpoint is where you look from.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Content Metamodel?
notes.back: A model defining the types of building blocks (entities) that may exist in an architecture and the relationships between them — providing a structured, consistent way to classify and store architecture content in the repository.

notes.front: Name the four characteristics that make a good building block.
notes.back: It should: be a package of functionality defined to meet business needs; have published interfaces; be loosely coupled / reusable and replaceable; and may interoperate with other building blocks. Building blocks can be specified at varying levels of detail.

notes.front: What is the Enterprise Continuum?
notes.back: A view and classification model of the Architecture Repository showing how architectures and solutions evolve from generic/foundational to specific/organisation-specific. It comprises the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum.

notes.front: List the four levels of the Architecture Continuum (generic → specific).
notes.back:
1. Foundation Architectures
  2. Common Systems Architectures
  3. Industry Architectures
  4. Organization-Specific Architectures

notes.front: List the four levels of the Solutions Continuum (generic → specific).
notes.back:
1. Foundation Solutions
  2. Common Systems Solutions
  3. Industry Solutions
  4. Organization-Specific Solutions

notes.front: How do the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum relate?
notes.back: The Architecture Continuum describes requirements and building-block specifications (ABBs); the Solutions Continuum describes implementations (SBBs) that realise them. Each architecture level guides and is populated by the corresponding solutions level.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Repository, and what does it hold?
notes.back: A holding area for all architecture output. It contains: the Architecture Metamodel, Architecture Capability, Architecture Landscape, Standards Information Base (SIB), Reference Library, Governance Log, and the Architecture Requirements Repository.

notes.front: What are the three levels of the Architecture Landscape?
notes.back:
• Strategic Architecture — long-term, broad, summary-level
  • Segment Architecture — detailed, organising a portfolio/segment
  • Capability Architecture — detailed, for a specific capability/solution to be delivered

notes.front: What is the Standards Information Base (SIB)?
notes.back: The part of the Architecture Repository that captures the standards with which new architectures must comply — including legal, industry, and organisation-specific standards and the products/services that conform to them.

notes.front: What is the Technical Reference Model (TRM)?
notes.back: A Foundation Architecture reference model providing a model and taxonomy of generic platform services and an application platform. It sits at the most generic level of the Architecture Continuum.

notes.front: What is the Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM)?
notes.back: A reference model derived from the TRM, focused on the application software space, addressing the Boundaryless Information Flow problem — enabling integrated information access across the enterprise.

notes.front: What is a Foundation Architecture?
notes.back: The most generic architecture in the Architecture Continuum — a set of generic services and functions (e.g., as captured in the TRM) that provide a foundation on which more specific architectures can be built.

notes.front: What is the standard structure/form of an Architecture Principle in TOGAF?
notes.back:
• Name
  • Statement — a concise, unambiguous rule
  • Rationale — the business benefits
  • Implications — the requirements and impacts of adopting it

notes.front: What five quality criteria should a good set of Architecture Principles meet?
notes.back: Understandable, Robust, Complete, Consistent, Stable.

notes.front: What is Gap Analysis in the ADM, and where is it applied?
notes.back: A technique to identify gaps between the Baseline and Target Architectures — which building blocks are eliminated, retained, or newly required — ensuring nothing is accidentally omitted. Applied at the end of the domain phases (B, C, D).

notes.front: What is a Business Scenario?
notes.back: A technique to discover and document business requirements by describing a business process/situation, the actors involved, the desired outcome, and the human and computer roles — keeping the architecture driven by real business needs.

notes.front: What is Capability-Based Planning?
notes.back: A business-planning technique focused on planning, engineering, and delivering strategic business capabilities. It gives a cross-functional view that bridges business strategy and project delivery within the ADM.

notes.front: What is the Business Transformation Readiness Assessment (BTRA)?
notes.back: A technique that evaluates the organisation's preparedness to undergo change using readiness factors, identifying risks to the transformation. Used in Phases A and E.

notes.front: In TOGAF Risk Management, what two risk states are tracked?
notes.back: Initial Level of Risk (before mitigation) and Residual Level of Risk (after mitigating actions). Risks are classified by Effect and Frequency to derive impact (Extremely High / High / Moderate / Low) and are tracked in a Risk Register.

notes.front: What is Interoperability in the TOGAF context, and its common categories?
notes.back: The ability to share information and services. Commonly categorised as Operational/Business, Information, and Technical interoperability. Defining interoperability requirements is a cross-phase technique.

notes.front: What is Architecture Partitioning?
notes.back: Dividing the enterprise architecture into partitions — by breadth (subject), depth (detail), time period, and maturity — to manage complexity and assign teams. It underpins the Strategic/Segment/Capability landscape levels.

notes.front: What is a Stakeholder Map (Power/Interest grid) used for?
notes.back: A stakeholder-management technique to classify stakeholders by their power and level of interest, so the architecture team can tailor engagement (e.g., manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor).

notes.front: What are Architecture Alternatives and Trade-offs used for in the ADM?
notes.back: A technique for evaluating multiple candidate architectures against requirements, principles, cost, risk, and value — making the selection of a Target Architecture an explicit, justifiable decision rather than an implicit one.

notes.front: What is Architecture Governance?
notes.back: The practice by which Enterprise Architectures are managed and controlled at an enterprise-wide level — covering the governance framework, compliance management, and control of work products via the Governance Log.

notes.front: What is the role of the Architecture Board?
notes.back: A cross-organisation governance body responsible for oversight of the architecture's implementation: ensuring consistency, managing compliance and dispensations, and acting as the focal point for governance decisions.

notes.front: List the levels of Architecture Compliance (conformance) in TOGAF.
notes.back: Irrelevant, Consistent, Compliant, Conformant, Fully Conformant, Non-Conformant — describing how an implementation/specification relates to the features of the architecture.

notes.front: What is a Dispensation in architecture governance?
notes.back: A time-bound, governed exemption granted when a project cannot (yet) comply with the architecture. It records the non-compliance, the agreed conditions, and an expiry by which compliance must be achieved or re-reviewed.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Capability Framework?
notes.back: Guidance and resources for establishing and operating an architecture function within an enterprise — roles, skills (the Architecture Skills Framework), governance structures, and the Architecture Board.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Skills Framework?
notes.back: A TOGAF framework defining the roles, skills, and proficiency levels expected of enterprise architects and related staff, used to assess and develop the organisation's architecture capability.

notes.front: What four characteristics underpin effective Architecture Governance?
notes.back: Discipline, Transparency, Independence (of accountability), and Accountability/Responsibility. (Often summarised with Fairness.) They ensure decisions are controlled, visible, and answerable.

notes.front: What is the "Request for Architecture Work" and where does it originate?
notes.back: A document requesting that architecture work begin. It is an output of the Preliminary Phase that triggers Phase A, sent from the sponsoring organisation to the architecture function.

notes.front: What is the "Statement of Architecture Work"?
notes.back: A deliverable defining the scope and approach for completing an architecture project — effectively the work plan/contract for the engagement. Produced and approved in Phase A.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Vision deliverable?
notes.back: A high-level, aspirational summary of the changes the work will produce, created early (Phase A) to gain stakeholder buy-in and communicate business value before detailed work begins.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Definition Document (ADD)?
notes.back: The deliverable holding the core architectural artifacts and narrative across all domains — both Baseline and Target for Business, Data, Application, and Technology. It is the qualitative companion to the Architecture Requirements Specification.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS)?
notes.back: A quantitative, measurable set of requirements the architecture must meet — the requirements companion to the (qualitative) Architecture Definition Document.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Roadmap?
notes.back: A list of individual work packages/increments laid out on a timeline to move from the Baseline to the Target Architecture. First assembled in Phase E and finalised in Phase F.

notes.front: What is the Implementation and Migration Plan?
notes.back: A deliverable providing the schedule for implementing the solution described by the Architecture Roadmap, coordinated with enterprise change management. Finalised in Phase F.

notes.front: What is a Capability Assessment deliverable?
notes.back: An evaluation of the enterprise's current and target capability (business, IT, and architecture maturity) used to understand readiness and gaps. Created in Phase A and used in Phase E.

notes.front: What is the Communications Plan?
notes.back: A deliverable ensuring stakeholders are kept informed — addressing their information needs, the frequency, and the methods of communication throughout the architecture work. Produced in Phase A.

notes.front: What is the Tailored Architecture Framework?
notes.back: The output of tailoring TOGAF (and other frameworks) to the enterprise — selected/tailored content, principles, and a configured method. Produced in the Preliminary Phase and refined in Phase A.

notes.front: What is the Compliance Assessment deliverable?
notes.back: A record produced during governance (Phase G) documenting how far a project's implementation conforms to the architecture, and any deviations or dispensations required.

notes.front: Name several domains covered by TOGAF Series Guides in the 10th-edition Library.
notes.back: Examples: Business Architecture (Business Capabilities, Value Streams, Organization/Information Mapping), Security Architecture, Information/Data Architecture, Agile methods, Digital, Government, Microservices Architecture, and the ADM Practitioners' approach. (Exact titles evolve over time.)

notes.front: In TOGAF Business Architecture, what is a Business Capability?
notes.back: A particular ability or capacity a business may possess or exchange to achieve a specific purpose — a stable description of what the business does, independent of how, who, or where.

notes.front: In TOGAF Business Architecture, what is a Value Stream?
notes.back: An end-to-end collection of value-adding activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user — representing the sequence by which value is delivered.

notes.front: What is Organization Mapping in TOGAF Business Architecture?
notes.back: A technique that depicts organisational units, partners, and stakeholders and relates them to capabilities and value streams — showing who is involved in delivering value.

notes.front: What is Information Mapping in TOGAF Business Architecture?
notes.back: A technique that links the information the business needs to its capabilities and value streams, providing the bridge from Business Architecture to the Data Architecture.

notes.front: What does "Applying the ADM" guidance address?
notes.back: How to adapt and use the ADM in practice — including iteration, applying it across the Architecture Landscape levels, security considerations, and using the Enterprise Continuum and repository. It is the practical-application document of the Fundamental Content.

notes.front: What is the relationship between the ADM and the Enterprise Continuum?
notes.back: As the ADM progresses, the architect moves from generic to specific along the continuum — reusing Foundation/Common Systems/Industry assets from the repository and producing Organization-Specific architectures and solutions that are fed back in.

notes.front: What is the Governance Log?
notes.back: The record within the Architecture Repository that captures governance activity — decisions, compliance assessments, dispensations, and Architecture Contracts — providing an audit trail for architecture governance.

notes.front: Why is security treated as a cross-cutting concern in the ADM?
notes.back: Security and risk requirements affect every domain and phase (business, data, application, technology) rather than a single phase, so the TOGAF Security Architecture guidance threads security considerations throughout the ADM cycle.

notes.front: What is an Architecture Maturity Model used for in TOGAF?
notes.back: To assess and benchmark the maturity of an organisation's architecture practice/capability (e.g., process, governance, skills), identifying where capability must improve. Often based on a Capability Maturity Model approach.
